Karthik, Monica —

I reviewed Acme's redlines. Summary and recommended positions below:

1) Prior written approval for subcontracting — not acceptable as drafted. It is too broad and subjective. Proposal: accept a limited approval right for (i) any new subprocessors that will have access to customer PII or customer prompt/content, and (ii) any cross-border transfers outside of North America/EU. For all other routine service providers (hosting in pre-approved cloud providers, CDN, monitoring, CI/CD) we will provide written notification only.

Suggested clause language (brief):
- Redwood will notify Customer of any new subprocessor with access to Customer Data at least 30 days prior to engagement. For subprocessors that will access Customer Data as described above, Customer may reasonably withhold approval only where the proposed subprocessor materially fails to meet Customer's security requirements; any such withholding must be specific and in writing within 15 business days.

2) Notice period for material change — Acme's edit reduces clarity on what "material" means. We propose 30 days notice for new subprocessors affecting data handling, and 10 business days for emergency or patch changes that do not affect the security posture.

3) Evidence requests / SOC2 access — reasonable to provide SOC2 report and DPA excerpts. Counter: agree to provide SOC2 Type II report and a copy of the subprocessor DPA on a confidential basis within 10 business days of a written request, provided Redwood is permitted to redact commercially sensitive terms (pricing, volume). If Acme requires direct audit rights of subprocessors, we should decline and offer summary attestations or a vendor questionnaire response instead.

4) Flow-down language — we should commit to flow down data protection obligations "to the extent applicable and commercially reasonable" and include audit/evidence mechanics. Avoid absolute language that requires subcontractors to accept identical liability caps or indemnities.

Next steps: I can produce a redline with the language above. Monica — can you confirm whether offering the limited approval right will impact the commercial terms or pricing (we should keep track of any elevated risk).

Lauren Bishop
Senior Counsel, Redwood Inference

Hi Olivia — thanks for the redlines and for the clear ask. We've reviewed internally with legal and have a path forward that should resolve procurement's concerns without imposing open-ended approval rights on Redwood. Key points we propose: 

- Subprocessor approvals: Redwood will provide 30 days' written notice for any new subprocessor engagement. For subprocessors that will process customer content or personal data outside of standard hosting, Acme may raise objections in writing within 15 business days; such objections must identify specific compliance/security deficiencies. Redwood will not subcontract to unauthorized parties while a legitimate objection is under review.

- Evidence & SOC2: Redwood will provide our SOC2 Type II report and a copy of the relevant subprocessor DPA within 10 business days of a written request. We will redact commercially sensitive fields (pricing, SLAs specific to other customers). If Acme requires additional audit rights, we'll propose a carve that allows for a vendor questionnaire and a SOC attestation rather than direct subprocessor audits.

- Flow-down commitments: Redwood will flow down data protection obligations to subprocessors to the extent reasonably practicable and will require subprocessors to enter DPA terms that are materially consistent with our commitments to Acme. We cannot accept a blanket requirement that subcontractors accept identical liability caps.

I've attached a short redline that implements the above and keeps the notice windows Acme requested where feasible. If that looks good we can finalize the MSA and push the Order Form to procurement. Happy to schedule a 30-minute call tomorrow to walk through the redline.

Best,
Karthik Iyer
Head of Sales, Redwood Inference
